name: CJC-1295 (No DAC)

b.x: The community figured this one out before the researchers did. CJC-1295 without DAC, also called Mod GRF 1-29 (parent GRF(1-29) CAS 83930-13-6), is a 29-amino-acid GHRH analog modified at four positions to resist enzymatic breakdown. Its closest human data comes from Corpas et al. (1992) [1], where GHRH(1-29) injected subcutaneously twice daily reversed the low GH and IGF-1 levels of old men. The mechanism is direct. Mod GRF 1-29 binds the GHRH receptor on pituitary somatotroph cells, triggering a cAMP-driven GH release that peaks around 15 to 30 minutes and clears within the hour. That short action window is the entire point. Unlike the DAC version (which circulates for days and produces tonic GH elevation), the no-DAC form preserves your natural pulsatile rhythm. Real-world use centers on the Mod GRF + Ipamorelin stack. Community consensus across hundreds of r/Peptides threads and practitioner networks puts the standard protocol at 100 mcg of each, co-injected subcutaneously once or twice daily on a fasted stomach before bed. Users consistently report improved sleep within the first two weeks, faster recovery by week three, and visible body composition changes by month two. Product quality is a known problem; Finnrick Analytics found purity as low as 68.75% across 244 samples from 47 companies. No FDA-approved form exists, and no Phase I, II, or III trial has been completed for Mod GRF 1-29 specifically.

Mod GRF 1-29 acts on one receptor, but the downstream cascade is worth understanding. The compound binds to the GHRH receptor (GHRHR) on anterior pituitary somatotroph cells. This is a Gs protein-coupled receptor. Binding activates adenylyl cyclase, raises intracellular cAMP, and primes the cell for GH synthesis and exocytosis. Its half-life has never been measured in people; the community estimate is roughly 30 minutes. The closest human data are for a related D-Ala2 analog (Soule et al.) [2]. Given by IV infusion to 10 men, it cleared with a 6.7-minute half-time. Either way, receptor exposure lasts only a brief window. That brevity produces a sharp GH spike that mimics the body's own pulsatile pattern; somatostatin feedback kicks in and shuts the pulse down naturally. When paired with Ipamorelin (a ghrelin mimetic acting on GHS-R1a), the two pathways converge on the same somatotroph cell from different directions. GHRH sets the amplitude. The ghrelin signal sets the timing. Community reports describe a combined GH pulse larger than either compound alone. Ipamorelin's selectivity matters here. Unlike GHRP-2 or GHRP-6, it doesn't elevate cortisol, ACTH, or prolactin at standard doses. Downstream, the raised GH pulse drives hepatic IGF-1 production, lipolysis through hormone-sensitive lipase activation, and anabolic signaling in muscle and connective tissue.
CJC-1295 (No DAC) benefits center on natural GH pulse amplification and the downstream effects that follow.
Pulsatile GH release that preserves your body's own feedback loops. Unlike the DAC form or exogenous HGH, somatostatin regulation stays intact (Corpas et al. 1992,; analog mechanism confirmed) [1].

Clean hormonal profile when stacked with Ipamorelin. No cortisol, ACTH, or prolactin elevation at 100 mcg doses; this selectivity is what separates the Ipamorelin pairing from GHRP-2 or GHRP-6 stacks (Raun et al. 1998) [3].

Improved sleep quality within 1 to 2 weeks. This is the most consistently reported early benefit across community protocols, with users noting deeper sleep and more vivid dreams before any body composition changes appear.

Gradual body composition improvement by months 2 to 3. Community reports describe reduced abdominal fat and improved muscle fullness, consistent with GH-mediated lipolysis and anabolic signaling observed in GRF(1-29) infusion literature.

Short half-life allows fine-grained protocol control. If side effects appear, the compound clears within hours. Compare that to CJC-1295 DAC, which sustains GH elevation for days after a single injection.

Reconstitution math for common vial sizes. A 2 mg vial with 2 mL bacteriostatic water gives you 1,000 mcg/mL. A 100 mcg dose is 10 units on an insulin syringe (0.1 mL). A 5 mg vial with 2 mL bacteriostatic water gives you 2,500 mcg/mL. A 100 mcg dose is 4 units (0.04 mL); a 200 mcg dose is 8 units (0.08 mL). The fasting window is non-negotiable. Two hours minimum with no food before injection; 30 minutes after. Insulin raises somatostatin, which shuts down the GH pulse completely. This is the number-one troubleshooting issue when users report no IGF-1 movement after weeks on protocol. Check fasting compliance before blaming the peptide. Abdominal subcutaneous injection absorbs faster than thigh or flank. For a compound with a 30-minute active window, that speed matters.
Cycling Protocol
Cycle to prevent pituitary desensitization. Some users run 5 days on, 2 days off weekly.
CJC-1295 (No DAC) Cycle

Chronic daily GHRH stimulation can shift somatostatin tone (the primary inhibitory counterbalance to GH release) and reduce pituitary somatotroph responsiveness over time. When stacked with Ipamorelin, GHS-R1a desensitization from the GHRP component adds a second desensitization mechanism. Community consensus and analog literature support 12-week on / 4-week off cycling. The short half-life (~30 min, estimated) means receptor exposure is only during the brief post-injection window, desensitization is slower than with the DAC form, but 16+ weeks of daily use without a break has produced reported diminishing returns in community experience.

CJC-1295 (DAC)

Combining DAC and no-DAC forms creates overlapping GHRHR stimulation with mismatched half-lives. The DAC form provides sustained tonic GHRH exposure that defeats the pulsatile rationale of no-DAC. No documented benefit; increased receptor desensitization risk.
Exogenous HGH (recombinant GH)

Combining GH secretagogues with exogenous HGH saturates the GH axis and suppresses endogenous pulsatility. Eliminates the primary rationale for using secretagogues (axis preservation). Dramatically increases IGF-1 overshoot risk.

The biggest safety concern with CJC-1295 (No DAC) is that zero completed clinical trials exist for this specific compound. Every side effect profile is extrapolated from analog studies and community experience. That context matters for everything below. Facial flushing is the most immediately noticeable effect. It typically hits within 5 to 15 minutes of injection, feels like a warm rush to the face and ears, and resolves within 30 to 60 minutes. This is a vasodilatory response from the GH pulse itself, not an allergic reaction. Community reports treat it as a sign the peptide is active. Reducing the dose lessens the intensity. Headache and dizziness occur in some users, usually during the first week. These tend to be transient and resolve as the body adjusts to regular GH pulses. Injection site redness and irritation are typical of any subcutaneous peptide; rotating sites prevents local tissue issues. Water retention is the side effect that gets the most community attention at higher dose frequencies. GH promotes sodium and water reabsorption. Mild puffiness around the hands and face is common, especially at twice-daily dosing. If retention becomes pronounced (visible edema, tight rings, swollen ankles), reduce frequency before reducing dose. Persistent edema warrants checking IGF-1 levels. Carpal tunnel symptoms (tingling, numbness in the hands, grip weakness) signal excessive GH-mediated fluid retention compressing the median nerve. This is a dose-dependent effect. Reduce dose immediately if it appears. If symptoms persist beyond one week at a lower dose, stop entirely and allow four or more weeks of recovery. GH release antagonizes insulin action. Anyone with diabetes, prediabetes, or insulin resistance should monitor fasting glucose carefully. Teichman et al. (2006) [4] documented insulin sensitivity effects with the DAC form; the no-DAC form carries the same mechanistic risk at lower magnitude due to shorter exposure. GH promotes cell proliferation. Active cancer or a history of malignancy is a contraindication. Pregnancy and breastfeeding are absolute contraindications. Untreated hypothyroidism can blunt the GH response entirely and should be addressed before starting. Product quality adds an underappreciated risk layer. Finnrick Analytics tested 244 samples from 47 companies and found purity ranging from 68.75% to 99.95%. Underdosed or degraded product produces unpredictable responses; the no-DAC form (MW approximately 3,367 Da) is sometimes substituted with the DAC form (MW approximately 3,647 Da) in low-quality products. When to see a doctor: carpal tunnel symptoms that don't resolve with dose reduction, persistent unexplained edema, fasting glucose above 125 mg/dL, or any new numbness or paresthesia.
Common Issues & Solutions

No IGF-1 change after 8 weeks: Most common cause is eating within 2 hours before injection: insulin raises somatostatin and blunts the GH pulse completely. Check fasting compliance first, then product quality (a batch-specific CoA is the only check).

Facial flushing within minutes of injection: Expected vasodilatory response from GH release. Usually peaks at 5–15 minutes, resolves within 30–60 minutes. Reduce dose if severe; does not indicate an allergic reaction in most cases.

Water retention / puffiness: Common with any GH secretagogue. Reduce injection frequency before reducing dose. If significant edema persists, stop and check IGF-1 levels: may indicate excessive GH response.

Diminishing response after week 8–10: Consistent with somatostatin tone accumulation and possible GHS-R1a desensitization (from Ipamorelin component). Consider cycling off 2 weeks early rather than pushing through. Ensure 4-week off period before restarting.

Tingling or numbness in hands: Early carpal tunnel symptom from GH-mediated fluid retention. Reduce dose or frequency immediately. If it persists more than 1 week at reduced dose, discontinue and allow 4+ weeks recovery.

CJC-1295 without DAC (Mod GRF 1-29) is sold as a research chemical in the United States. It has no FDA approval for any indication. FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) voted against adding CJC-1295 (free base and acetate) to the 503A bulks list on December 4, 2024. The vote is advisory, and FDA has not ruled on the listing. CJC-1295 is not on the 503A bulks list (21 CFR 216.23). FDA's Category 2 page lists CJC-1295 as withdrawn by its nominators and notes serious adverse events, including increased heart rate and a systemic vasodilatory reaction. For athletes, both CJC-1295 and Ipamorelin appear on the WADA prohibited list under S2 (Peptide Hormones, Growth Factors, Related Substances, and Mimetics). Anti-doping labs have built urine tests for CJC-1295 using spiked samples [5], and one was validated to WADA standards [6]. It is sold online under "for research purposes only" labeling. No GMP manufacturing requirement applies. This content is for educational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice. Consult a qualified healthcare provider before using any peptide.

faqs.q: If I inject Mod GRF 3x daily, does the third pulse still produce a meaningful GH response?
faqs.a: The pituitary requires ~3+ hours between stimulations for meaningful recovery. If three daily doses are spaced at least 3 hours apart, each should produce a GH pulse. Community reports suggest diminishing returns on the third daily injection, possibly because somatostatin feedback accumulates through the day. No clinical data exists for the no-DAC form specifically.

faqs.q: Why aren't my IGF-1 levels moving after 8 weeks on Mod GRF + Ipamorelin?
faqs.a: Most common causes in order: eating within 2 hours of injection (completely blunts the GH pulse), degraded or underdosed peptide (only a CoA can rule this out), individual baseline IGF-1 already near the ceiling for your age, or insufficient dose frequency. Troubleshoot fasting first, then product quality.

faqs.q: Can I use Mod GRF 1-29 on TRT: does it interact with testosterone or estradiol?
faqs.a: No pharmacokinetic interactions with exogenous testosterone are established. The practical concern is combined IGF-1 + testosterone anabolic signaling, which may require more careful IGF-1 monitoring. No clinical trial data covers this combination.

faqs.q: Does Mod GRF 1-29 suppress natural GHRH production through negative feedback?
faqs.a: GHRH secretagogues are broadly considered more axis-friendly than direct HGH injections because they preserve GH feedback loops; somatostatin still responds, keeping regulation in place. However, chronic daily use can alter pulsatile patterns and potentially shift somatostatin tone. There is no definitive clinical answer for the no-DAC version.

faqs.q: Does injection site (abdomen vs. thigh vs. flank) matter for GH pulse timing?
faqs.a: Abdominal subcutaneous injection typically has faster absorption than thigh or flank, which is preferable for a compound with a ~30-minute active window. Community consensus favors abdominal SC injection for both Mod GRF and Ipamorelin. No clinical comparison of injection sites exists for this compound.

faqs.q: What is the recommended CJC-1295 (No DAC) dosage?
faqs.a: CJC-1295 (No DAC) dosing varies by experience level. Beginners typically start at 100 mcg daily, moderate users at 100 mcg 2x daily, and aggressive protocols use 200 mcg 2x daily.

faqs.q: How do you reconstitute CJC-1295 (No DAC)?
faqs.a: CJC-1295 (No DAC) typically comes in 2mg or 5mg vials. Add 2mL of bacteriostatic water to the vial. Use the free calculator for exact syringe units based on your desired dose.

summary: Zero completed clinical trials for this specific compound, and it's still the most popular GHRH analog in the peptide community. CJC-1295 without DAC (Mod GRF 1-29) is a short-acting growth hormone-releasing hormone analog with a half-life estimated at about 30 minutes. No human study has measured it. It triggers a GH pulse that rises and falls the way your pituitary does on its own, then clears. The 100 mcg dosing convention comes from receptor saturation modeling and community experience across 300 to 600 Reddit threads, not from a clinical trial.
